article.headline: Delvaux Turns Death's Medieval Procession Into a Dream
article.lede: The *danse macabre* — Death personified as skeleton, escorting pope and peasant alike toward the grave — is one of the great recurring images of Western art, born from the anxieties of plague-era Europe. Paul Delvaux, who spent a career collapsing the distance between the erotic and the morbid, returned to the motif in February 1959 with pen, ink, gouache, and wash on card. What he produced was not a *memento mori* in any traditional sense — it was something stranger and quieter.
article.body:
Paul Delvaux (1897–1994) spent the 1950s in an extended, unsentimental reckoning with the skeleton. After a 1934 encounter with Giorgio de Chirico's *metaphysical painting* cracked open his imagination, he built a career on dreamlike tableaux: nude or semi-nude women in trance states wandering through classical ruins and railway stations flooded in moonlight. By the early 1950s, skeletons began appearing alongside them — first in a series of Passion paintings and Crucifixions in which he replaced Christ and the mourners with animated bone figures. The Patriarch of Venice condemned the series as blasphemous. Delvaux, characteristically unmoved, acquired an actual skeleton to use as a studio model.

His attraction to bone, he explained, was not about death but about foundation — the skeleton as the armature beneath living skin, animated rather than cadaverous. Critics noted that his skeletons were always "devoid of funereal meaning." In *L'Hiver* (1952), they sleep peacefully in a hothouse among blooming plants. The impulse was closer to wonder than to terror.

**La danse macabre** (February 1959) sits within this meditation. The *danse macabre* is a medieval visual tradition — originating in a lost mural at the Holy Innocents' Cemetery in Paris around 1424 and codified in Hans Holbein the Younger's 41-woodcut series of 1538 — in which Death, as skeleton, escorts representatives of every social rank, from pope to ploughman, toward the grave. The tradition was a *memento mori*: a reminder that rank confers no exemption. Where Holbein's Death is a relentless choreographer of social leveling, Delvaux passes the motif through his own dreamworld: the dance becomes something hallucinatory, absorbed into the theatrical silence that surrounds his sleeping women and gas-lit trains. A 2015 Thyssen-Bornemisza retrospective, co-organized with the Musée d'Ixelles in Brussels, devoted an entire thematic section to this strand of his work, pairing his "Dance of Death" imagery explicitly with the Freudian coupling of *Eros and Thanatos* — suggesting that the work's energy comes precisely from the tension between fertility and dissolution.

The 1959 date carries its own context. That same year, Delvaux was completing *Le paradis terrestre*, a mural for Brussels's Palais des Congrès measuring 42 by 4.5 metres — one of the largest commissions of his career. The small card sheet (59.5 × 75 cm) of *La danse macabre*, worked in pen and ink with *gouache* and wash, is an intimate counterpart to that public ambition: the same iconographic vocabulary compressed into a more immediate, graphic register. The work descended through the artist's cousin Walter Delvaux and appeared twice at Sotheby's London — in 2014 and 2022 — with estimates across the two sales ranging from £18,000 to £40,000; its authenticity was confirmed by the Fondation Paul Delvaux.

Delvaux sits in the permanent shadow of his fellow Belgian René Magritte, whose auction record reached £59.4m in 2022. Delvaux's most sought paintings have sold for £3–6.6m at auction, but his works on paper occupy a more accessible tier. What *La danse macabre* offers — beyond market considerations — is a window into an artist's long, patient reckoning with death as image: not sermon, not terror, but one more figure in a procession that never quite ends.

concepts.definition: A medieval visual and literary tradition in which Death, personified as a skeleton, summons representatives of every social rank — pope, emperor, merchant, peasant — to dance toward the grave. Originating in late-14th- or early-15th-century Europe and shaped by the devastation of the Black Death, it served as a memento mori and an implicit social critique: no earthly rank escapes death. Hans Holbein the Younger's 41-woodcut series (published 1538) is its most celebrated visual expression.

An early-20th-century Italian movement associated primarily with Giorgio de Chirico. It depicted deserted piazzas, elongated shadows, classical architecture, and mannequin-like figures to evoke a dreamlike strangeness beneath ordinary reality. Delvaux encountered de Chirico's work at a Brussels exhibition in 1934, an event he described as liberating his imagination from rationalist logic.

Latin for 'remember you must die.' A category of artistic object or image intended to remind the viewer of mortality. In painting, it encompasses skulls, hourglasses, wilting flowers, and — in the medieval tradition — the figure of Death itself, all deployed to encourage spiritual reflection on life's brevity.

The pairing, drawn from Freudian psychoanalytic theory, of the life instinct (Eros) and the death drive (Thanatos). In cultural criticism, it describes works that hold erotic and morbid impulses in simultaneous tension — a framework frequently applied to Delvaux, whose paintings combine sensual female figures with skeletal presences in the same scene.

An opaque, water-soluble paint with a higher pigment-to-binder ratio than watercolour, producing dense, matte areas of colour. Frequently used for works on paper, it allows for crisp lines and solid colour fields that watercolour cannot achieve, and can be combined with pen and ink to produce tonal and linear effects simultaneously.

An art-market and curatorial category encompassing drawings, prints, watercolours, gouaches, and mixed-media pieces on a paper or card support, as opposed to oil paintings on canvas. Works on paper by the same artist typically occupy a lower price tier at auction than their painted counterparts, though they can offer comparable artistic density and intimacy.
